lead: Entropy measures how many microscopic arrangements fit the same macroscopic state. Two samples can have the same energy, volume and number of particles yet very different numbers of ways to arrange those particles. Boltzmann turned that count into a number: S = kB ln Ω. The idea exists because the Clausius definition from entropy and the Clausius inequality tells you how entropy changes, but not what entropy is counting. Engineers use it to judge disorder in alloys, glasses and crystals, and to connect the third law to a real solid.
prereq: You need entropy as a state property from entropy and the Clausius inequality and the third law from third law.

blocks.text: A microstate is one exact arrangement of the particles in a system. For a gas, it fixes the position and momentum of every molecule. For a simple model, it can be as coarse as naming which half of a box each labelled molecule occupies. A macrostate is what you can measure: U, V and N, or in the box model just how many molecules are in the left half. Many microstates can give the same macrostate.

Take four labelled molecules and a box split into two equal halves. Each molecule can be left or right, so there are 2⁴ = 16 microstates. The macrostate "n molecules on the left" can be made in Ω = 4!/[n!(4 − n)!] ways: 1, 4, 6, 4 and 1 ways for n = 0 to 4. The even split has the most microstates, which is why a gas left to itself spreads evenly.

The basic assumption of statistical thermodynamics is that, at fixed U, V and N, every accessible microstate is equally likely. Entropy is then fixed by how many microstates are accessible. Liquid water has many more ways to share its thermal energy than ice, which is why the liquid has higher entropy.

blocks.where: S is entropy in J/K; k<sub>B</sub> = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K is the Boltzmann constant; ln is the natural logarithm; Ω is the number of accessible microstates at fixed U, V and N, dimensionless and at least 1.

blocks.text: The logarithm makes entropy additive. Two independent systems have Ω = Ω₁ Ω₂, so S = k<sub>B</sub> ln(Ω₁ Ω₂) = k<sub>B</sub> ln Ω₁ + k<sub>B</sub> ln Ω₂ = S₁ + S₂. Entropy of the pair is the sum, as thermodynamics demands.

When Ω = 1, ln 1 = 0 and S = 0. A single possible arrangement carries no entropy. Doubling Ω adds k<sub>B</sub> ln 2 = 0.693 k<sub>B</sub>, about 9.57 × 10⁻²⁴ J/K, whatever the starting count. For 1 mol of gas whose volume doubles, each of the N<sub>A</sub> molecules gets twice as many places, Ω rises by 2<sup>N<sub>A</sub></sup>, and ΔS = N<sub>A</sub> k<sub>B</sub> ln 2 = R ln 2 = 5.76 J/K: the same number the Clausius route gives in the chapter on entropy and the Clausius inequality.

At absolute zero a perfect crystal has every atom in its lowest-energy position. There is one way to build that crystal, so Ω = 1 and S = kB ln 1 = 0. This is the microscopic reason for the third law: perfect crystals have zero entropy at 0 K.

Some real solids never reach that single arrangement. Carbon monoxide molecules can point in two directions in the crystal, and cooling locks in a random mixture. Ice has protons arranged with many equivalent hydrogen-bond patterns; Pauling counted them and found S(0) = R ln(3/2) = 3.37 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, close to the measured value. A glass is frozen in a liquid-like arrangement. Each has Ω > 1 even at 0 K, so S = kB ln Ω gives a positive residual entropy. The third law is not broken; the crystal is simply not perfect.

Entropy is not merely 'disorder'. A system can look messy but have few accessible microstates, or look ordered but have many. The correct statement is: entropy counts accessible microstates at fixed U, V and N. Some syllabi call this the statistical interpretation of entropy.

examples.question: Four labelled gas molecules move in a box with two equal halves. (a) Find Ω for each macrostate n = 0 to 4 (n molecules on the left). (b) Find S/k<sub>B</sub> for the all-left macrostate, the even split and the whole box. (c) Find ΔS when 1 mol of ideal gas doubles its volume at constant temperature.
steps: Each molecule has 2 choices, so the whole box has 2⁴ = 16 microstates.
All on the left: S/k<sub>B</sub> = ln 1 = 0. Even split: S/k<sub>B</sub> = ln 6 = 1.792. Whole box: S/k<sub>B</sub> = ln 16 = 2.773.
One mole doubling its volume: Ω₂/Ω₁ = 2<sup>N<sub>A</sub></sup>, so ΔS = k<sub>B</sub> N<sub>A</sub> ln 2 = R ln 2 = 8.314 × 0.6931 = 5.76 J/K.
examples.answer: Ω = 1, 4, 6, 4, 1; S/k<sub>B</sub> = 0, 1.792 and 2.773; ΔS = R ln 2 = 5.76 J/K for 1 mol, matching the thermodynamic result.

print(round(8.314*math.log(2),2))

traps: Entropy is not just 'disorder'; it is the count of accessible microstates at fixed U, V and N. A visually messy system can have low entropy if few arrangements are accessible.
Ω is a count of microstates, not a probability and not work. It is dimensionless and cannot be less than 1.

R = N<sub>A</sub> k<sub>B</sub>. Use S = k<sub>B</sub> ln Ω for the whole system; per mole, S = R ln w only when each molecule independently has w arrangements (CO in a crystal, w = 2), because then Ω = w<sup>N<sub>A</sub></sup>.
S = 0 at 0 K only for a perfect crystal with a unique ground state. Glasses, CO and ice can keep residual entropy.
Do not say 'entropy is the number of microstates'; entropy is proportional to ln Ω, so it is not Ω itself. Doubling Ω does not double S.

quiz.q: Write the Boltzmann entropy relation and define every symbol.
quiz.a: S = k<sub>B</sub> ln Ω, where S is entropy in J/K, k<sub>B</sub> = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K is the Boltzmann constant, and Ω is the number of accessible microstates at fixed U, V and N (dimensionless, Ω ≥ 1).

quiz.q: Why does entropy increase when Ω increases?
quiz.a: More accessible microstates mean the macrostate can be realised in more ways; the logarithm makes entropy count those ways and grow with Ω.

quiz.q: Two independent systems have Ω₁ = 10 and Ω₂ = 100. Find the total Ω and total S/k<sub>B</sub>.
At fixed U, V and N a system has Ω = 8. Find S/k<sub>B</sub> and S using k<sub>B</sub> = 1.381 × 10⁻²³ J/K.
Ω changes from 100 to 200 at fixed U, V and N. Find the change in entropy.
quiz.a: ΔS = k<sub>B</sub> ln(200/100) = k<sub>B</sub> ln 2 = 0.693 × 1.381 × 10⁻²³ = 9.57 × 10⁻²⁴ J/K. It is positive.

quiz.q: A perfect crystal and a glass are both at 0 K. Which has S = 0 and why may the other not?
quiz.a: The perfect crystal has one ground-state arrangement, Ω = 1, so S = k<sub>B</sub> ln 1 = 0. The glass is frozen in many equivalent arrangements, Ω > 1, so it keeps residual entropy S = k<sub>B</sub> ln Ω > 0.

quiz.q: Give one reason 'entropy is disorder' is a poor definition. Use the Boltzmann relation.
quiz.a: Disorder is visual and vague. Boltzmann entropy depends on the number of accessible microstates at fixed U, V and N. A system can look ordered but have many accessible arrangements, or look messy but have few, so the count, not the appearance, sets S.

quiz.q: Name two real solids that can show residual entropy at 0 K.
quiz.a: Carbon monoxide (CO) crystals and ice (or a glass) are standard examples; both freeze in many equivalent arrangements.

beyond: Not for the exam. Statistical mechanics builds the whole of thermodynamics from Ω: the partition function, Boltzmann distribution and quantum gases all start here. Materials science uses configurational entropy to model alloys and solid solutions; cryogenics uses residual entropy to check whether a solid has truly ordered. Search next for 'configurational entropy', 'residual entropy of ice' and 'Boltzmann distribution'. A later course derives S = k<sub>B</sub> ln Ω from probability rather than stating it.
